title: Sexual Violence/Abuse and Cervical Cancer: A Systematic Review of the Relationship
abstract: Sexual violence/abuse may influence cervical carcinogenesis through increased human papillomavirus exposure, trauma-related immune dysregulation and reduced engagement with prevention and care. However, the evidence on the co-occurrence of cervical cancer and sexual violence/abuse has not been systematically synthesised. MEDLINE, PsycINFO, CINAHL Plus, PsycArticles, EMBASE and Scopus were searched for English-language studies published between January 2000 and January 2025. Studies were eligible if they reported the prevalence of cervical cancer among survivors of sexual violence/abuse or vice versa. Risk of bias was assessed using Joanna Briggs Institute critical appraisal tools. Seven studies from community, primary care and gynaecological oncology settings met inclusion criteria, covering a population of 8,840 participants. Among survivors of sexual violence/abuse, cervical cancer prevalence ranged from 5.4% to 32.3% and was consistently 1.5 to 2.7 times higher than among non-exposed comparators within the same settings. Among cervical cancer populations, sexual violence/abuse prevalence ranged from 18.4% to 57.5%, with stronger associations observed for severe or penetrative exposures. Adjusted odds ratios and relative risks ranged from approximately 3.3 to 11.15 at the highest exposure levels, consistent with a dose-response pattern. Findings point to a need for prevention strategies that consider how gender intersects with exposure to sexual violence/abuse. The review also suggests elevated co-occurrence between cervical cancer and sexual violence/abuse relative to global population estimates (~10% intimate-partner violence and ~6% non-partner violence). Limitations include small samples and measurement heterogeneity. Findings support co-produced, survivor-centred and trauma-informed approaches to cervical cancer prevention and oncology care that address barriers to healthcare engagement. Larger studies using validated measures and confounder-aware designs are needed.
